prompt: You add the check `if left[-1] <= right[0]: return left + right` (skip the merge) to merge sort. On already sorted input of 1,024 elements, how many element comparisons does the whole sort make?

options.explanation: Correct. A binary recursion with 1,024 leaves has 1,023 internal nodes (merge calls). Each check succeeds immediately, so each costs exactly one comparison.

options.text: 10,240: input size times its base-two logarithm
options.explanation: That ignores the shortcut. Every merge is skipped after one comparison, so comparison cost per merge is O(1); copying the concatenated halves still costs O(size).

options.text: 10: the base-two logarithm of the input size
options.explanation: There are many merge calls per level (512 at the bottom), and each needs its own check.

options.text: 5,120, using half the input size times its base-two logarithm
options.explanation: That is plain merge sort's comparison count on sorted input, without the shortcut.

workedExample:
1. The recursion tree for 1,024 elements is a full binary tree with 1,024 leaves.
2. A full binary tree has one fewer internal node than leaves:

```formula
N = L − 1
N = 1024 − 1 = 1023
where
N: the number of internal nodes, which are the merge calls
L: the number of leaves, one per element; here 1,024
In words: every merge joins two pieces into one, so turning 1,024 pieces into 1 takes 1,023 merges.
```
3. On sorted input, the last element of the left half is always ≤ the first of the right, so each merge is skipped after 1 comparison.
4. Total: 1,023 comparisons, linear in the number of elements. (Copying the concatenated halves still costs time unless it is done in place, as in array implementations that simply return.)

This one check is a cheap way to make merge sort adaptive for sorted input.

prompt:
You are choosing between merge sort and quicksort for a new job. Which of these are good reasons to pick **merge sort**? Select all that apply.

Here n is the number of input elements; other symbols are defined in this question’s formula cards. Big O is an asymptotic upper bound; Θ and Ω denote matching growth and a lower bound.

options.text: Records with equal keys must keep their original order
options.explanation: Correct. Merge sort is stable; standard quicksort is not, because partitioning swaps elements over long distances.

options.text: The data is in files on disk and must be read sequentially
options.explanation: Correct. Merge sort's passes and k-way merges read and write sequentially, which is why external sorting is merge-based.

options.text: You need a guaranteed worst case of O(n log n) without extra tricks
options.explanation: Correct (n is the number of elements). Plain quicksort is O(n²) in the worst case; merge sort is n log n on every input.

options.text: Memory is very tight and the data is an array
options.explanation: This favours quicksort or heapsort. Array merge sort needs an O(n) buffer.

options.text: You want the fastest in-memory sort of random integers
options.explanation: Quicksort-family algorithms can benefit from in-place sequential partitioning, but the fastest choice depends on implementation, data and hardware; this requirement alone does not establish merge sort as the best choice.

workedExample:
Match each requirement to the algorithms' properties:

| Need | Merge | Quick |
|---|---|---|
| Stable | Yes | No |
| Sequential I/O | Yes | No |
| Worst-case O(n log n) | Yes | No (plain) |
| O(1)–O(log n) memory | No | Yes |
| Raw speed in RAM | Measure | Measure |

The first three favour merge sort; the last two favour quicksort. That is exactly why Java uses TimSort (merge-based) for objects, where stability matters, and quicksort for primitives.
